plan.contextChunk: This figure shows two rose curves plotted on separate polar grids, set side by side and labeled (a) and (b) beneath. Each grid is built from dotted concentric circles crossed by dotted radial spokes, with solid horizontal and vertical axes arrowed at all four ends. Panel (a) holds a teal curve of eight identical petals, all springing from the origin at equal angular intervals so that four lie along the axes and four along the diagonals between them; its caption reads r = acos(n theta), n even. Panel (b) holds a curve in the same teal weight but with only three petals, one pointing straight down along the negative vertical axis and the other two angled up to the left and up to the right, spaced a third of a turn apart; its caption reads r = asin(n theta), n odd. Every petal reaches out to roughly the same radius, so each curve fills a circular envelope. Setting the panels side by side isolates the parity of n as the only thing governing the count: an even n produces 2n petals while an odd n produces just n, and the eight-petal and three-petal drawings are the two cases of that rule.

interactionPlan.concept: In a polar rose r = a·cos(nθ) or r = a·sin(nθ), the parity of n governs the petal count (n petals if n is odd, 2n petals if n is even), while a controls only the size and sine versus cosine only the orientation.
elements: polar grid: dotted concentric circles at increasing radii
dotted radial spokes at regular angular intervals
solid horizontal and vertical axes with arrowheads at all four ends
teal rose curve drawn from the origin, petals of equal length reaching the outer radius a
equation label beneath the grid: r = a·cos(nθ) or r = a·sin(nθ) with current a and n values
live readout showing petal count and whether n is even or odd

interactions.label: n (integer)
interactions.teaches: Stepping n through integers reveals the parity rule directly: odd n yields n petals, even n yields 2n petals — the count is governed by n alone

interactions.label: Trig form
interactions.teaches: Switching between cosine and sine rotates the entire rose (petals shift between axis-aligned and diagonal orientations) without changing the petal count — orientation is independent of the parity rule

interactions.label: a (amplitude)
interactions.teaches: Changing a scales every petal to a new maximum radius while the number and arrangement of petals stay fixed — a controls size, not count

demo_steps.title: The original figures
demo_steps.narration: Start with the cosine rose at n = 4, matching panel (a): an even n produces 2n = 8 petals, four on the axes and four on the diagonals.

demo_steps.title: Odd n: the other case
demo_steps.narration: Switch to the sine form at n = 3, matching panel (b): an odd n produces only n = 3 petals, one pointing straight down. The petal count drops from 2n to n — parity, not size, is what changed.

demo_steps.title: Sweep n and watch the rule
demo_steps.narration: Drag n from 1 to 8: counts go 1, 4, 3, 8, 5, 12, 7, 16. Every even value doubles its petals while every odd value keeps exactly n — the parity rule is visible, not memorized.

demo_steps.title: Orientation vs. size
demo_steps.narration: Toggle between cosine and sine and then drag a: the rose rotates under the trig toggle and grows under a, but the petal count never changes. Orientation, size, and count are three independent controls.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The parity of n alone sets the petal count — odd n gives n petals, even n gives 2n petals — while a only scales the rose and sine/cosine only rotates it.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Render a single polar grid (the two panels of the original collapse into one interactive figure) with dotted concentric circles and dotted radial spokes, plus solid arrowed horizontal and vertical axes. Draw the rose in a medium-weight teal stroke, unfilled, all petals springing from the origin and reaching radius a. Cosine form places a petal on the positive horizontal axis; sine form rotates the pattern so that for n odd a petal points along the negative vertical axis. Show a caption-style equation label below the grid that updates with the current form, a, and n, plus a small readout like 'n = 4 (even) → 8 petals'. Smoothly redraw the curve as controls change.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Button/state for integer n: the learner steps through n values, the polar curve redraws with n petals for odd n and 2n petals for even n, making the parity rule visible instead of memorized.
- Toggle between cosine and sine forms: the learner switches r = a cos(n theta) and r = a sin(n theta), the rose rotates to a new orientation while the petal-count rule remains tied to n, separating orientation from parity.
- Slider for amplitude a: the learner changes a, every petal grows or shrinks to a new maximum radius without changing the number of petals, showing that a controls size rather than count.
- Equation input for the polar rose: learner edits r = a*cos(n*theta) or r = a*sin(n*theta), with fields for a and n; the graph redraws and petal count plus orientation update immediately.

authoredContext:
The formulas that generate the graph of a rose curve are given by r=acosnθ and r=asinnθ where a≠0. If n is even, the curve has 2n petals. If n is odd, the curve has n petals. See the figure.

Graph of two rose curves side by side. (A) is r=acos(ntheta), where n is even. Eight petals extending from origin, equally spaced. (B) is r=asin(ntheta) where n is odd. Three petals extending from the origin, equally spaced.

evaluation.notes: The default state faithfully reproduces panel (a) — an 8-petal cosine rose on a dotted polar grid with solid arrowed axes — and the sin(nθ) toggle plus demo steps correctly recreate panel (b)'s 3-petal rose with the down-pointing petal; the parity rule (even n → 2n petals, odd n → n petals) is implemented exactly right.
